atoms.text: The immortal jellyfish: under stress, an adult reverts to its juvenile polyp stage, so aging can run backward.
Transdifferentiation: specialized cells become other cell types, so the body rewrites its own history.
The stress trigger: injury, illness, or old age causes the reversion, so catastrophe is also an escape hatch.
The clone colony: all polyps from one larva are genetically identical, so immortality belongs to the lineage rather than the individual.
Theoretically endless: the cycle can repeat indefinitely, so death is an accident rather than a law.
The predator that still dies: most individuals are eaten before they can revert, so immortality is conditional on avoiding violence.
The jellyfish that eats jellyfish: the mature form preys on its relatives, so the immortal stage is also a cannibal.
The research subject: the species is studied for aging and pharmaceuticals, so its gift becomes a resource for others.
The reversion that erases: returning to polyp form discards the mature body and its experiences, so immortality costs memory.
The budding: new medusae bud off the polyp colony, so reproduction is also resurrection.
The invasive traveler: the jellyfish spreads through ballast water and blooms worldwide, so immortality enables colonization.
The tiny giant: the animal is only millimeters wide, so a world-changing power is packaged in something almost invisible.
The scientist who cannot tell species apart: two populations were long confused, so the discovery of difference changes what counts as a kind.
The biological immortality that is not personal: the individual can reset, but the self that resets is not the same, so the story asks what survives.
The polyp that waits: the sedentary stage can outlast a crisis, so patience is a survival strategy.
The specimen named after a patron: the species carries the name of a benefactor, so even immortality is branded.
